This paper focuses on solving polynomial linear systems with coefficient evaluation errors. The input involves polynomials of total degree at most $\delta$ over a field $\K$, where each is defined by multivariate polynomials of total degree $\delta'$ over $\K[\epsilon]$ ($\epsilon$ being the informal parameter for small quantities), and where every coefficient contains an error bounded in absolute value by $\eta \ll 1$. The solution itself consists of rational functions of $\epsilon$ evaluated at $\epsilon=1$ (where the denominator evaluates to a non-zero constant). The goal is to output an approximation of this solution where the absolute error is bounded by a given $\varepsilon$.

Drawing on recent advances showing that the condition number can be exponentially dependent on $\varepsilon^{-1}\eta^{-1}$ rather than just $\varepsilon^{-1}\eta^{-1}$, we present two primary algorithms. The first employs fast numerical techniques to compute an $\varepsilon$-approximation in time $T_1 = \tildeO(T_{gen}\cdot \kappa^2 \cdot \varepsilon^{-1}\eta^{-1})$. The second utilizes fast symbolic techniques to find the same approximation in time $T_2 = \tildeO(\text{cost of generic computation})$. The paper argues that the respective outcomes of these algorithms correspond to distinct practical applications.

A key contribution involves a method for "early termination" in the numerical approach.

This study investigates the emission characteristics of a Bessel beam organized into even and odd orbital angular momentum (OAM) pairs within a nonlinear medium characterized by cubic nonlinearities and parity-time (PT) symmetry. When driven by such a structured beam, the PT-symmetry-conserving bidirectional bound states exhibit oscillatory dynamics; specifically, under the influence of a pair with even OAM parity, the oscillatory cycle is significantly prolonged. In contrast, interaction with an OM pair results in nearly stationary oscillations. Furthermore, this even OAM configuration preserves the bidirectional nature of the oscillations for a more extended duration before undergoing directional breaking. In contrast to systems without even OAM, an odd OAM system exhibits directionality breaking after relatively short timescales. However, while final states may converge to unidirectional emission in both scenarios, the even OAM setup sustains its symmetric oscillatory behavior for substantially longer periods.

This study investigates the spectral properties of vector mesons within a thermal background characterized by chiral imbalance, a state where left- and right-handed fermions exhibit unequal chemical potentials. This inequality shifts the vacuum for charged mesons but leaves the neutral meson vacuum unchanged. By applying vector meson dominance (VMD) and utilizing finite-temperature density matrix theory with linear system approximation, we derive analytical expressions for the decay widths of both charged and neutral $\rho$ mesons. The resulting decay widths depend explicitly on this chemical imbalance parameter; consequently, the non-zero value contributes to modifications in the spectral function density for $\rho$ mesons.

We investigate the fundamental task of network size estimation, where distributed nodes in a network collaborate via message exchange to derive a size approximation. Focusing on the Byzantine fault model, where malicious nodes may act arbitrarily, we demonstrate that secure size estimation is fundamentally unachievable for constant-size networks. To address this, we introduce new network anti-dos mechanisms that counter attacks by limited numbers of adversaries, specifically enabling the estimation of sub-exponentially growing network sizes. These mechanisms build upon existing one-way function techniques and yield a significant scaling improvement over current constant-growth algorithms. Furthermore, we examine the reverse scenario of super-exponential growth, designing methods for quantifying the volume of data attached to each node to reconstruct node counts. Collectively, these contributions establish fresh performance benchmarks for network size estimation security and efficiency within constant-growth environments under attack.

Numerical relativity simulations involving numerical black hole mergers typically begin with data satisfying all constraints when solving for two bodies on the largest orbit possible before their tidal forces cause them to merge. Generating this initial data requires solving a set of nonlinear partial differential equations. While many methods exist that satisfy both the momentum and Hamiltonian constraints simultaneously, this paper details a new technique called the "Constraint Trans-Thomas Fermi-Karman" (CTTK). This CTTK method stands out because it can enforce these constraints of initial data step-by. This approach offers many benefits, including making momentum constraint solution unnecessary and simplifying the Hamiltonian constraint into a linear form. This linear form can be solved using well-known methods like finite difference or spectral methods. This paper will detail this method mathematically and show results from testing this method with test cases.

The main experimental aim of the JUNO project is detecting neutrinos via the elastic scattering between solar, reactor, or accelerator-produced $C1$ neutrinos and targets to measure the two mass model parameters. JUNO is designed as a next-generation neutrino experiment featuring 20 tonnes of liquid scintillator (LS) within the largest single-phase detector ever built. Located 53–55 km south of the CNP5 nuclear reactor stack in the JUNO site near the city of Zhongshan, JUNO will monitor an elongated source like CNP5 over three distinct operational phases, anticipated to last approximately 3 to 6.5 years per stage. This observation strategy is projected to yield a $3\sigma$ measurement of the neutrino oscillation parameter $\Delta m^2_{32}$ within the first 15 years. Building on prior 14.5-month testing of initial photomultiplier components from March to April 2020, the most current campaign involved quality-assurance (QA) inspections for 3,058 of the 7,880 $20$-inch photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) scheduled for JUNO deployment. These $20$-inch PMTs were selected for their superior photoelectron yield and low noise characteristics. The present study details the measurement protocols and outcomes from this latest QA campaign.

Long short-term dependent data is frequently observed in multidimensional temporal sequences across diverse domains such as traffic monitoring, weather forecasting, and financial markets. Accurately estimating future values poses significant difficulties due to inherent nonlinearity, sparse data, and infrequent patterns. Although many innovative algorithms have addressed these issues, current methods often rely on overly rigid assumptions regarding data distributions, which hinders their generalization capability. Furthermore, most existing approaches fail to uncover the interdependencies between distinct time series or account for varying seasonalities and trends. Consequently, this study introduces a new Adaptive Graph Convolutional Network (AGCN) designed to model long-term dependencies effectively by synthesizing temporal dynamics with inter-series relationships. Furthermore, we decompose the intricate forecasting task into two interpretable subproblems: inferring the underlying structure of the time series collaterals and constructing an appropriate regression model. Crucially, we address the challenge of learning the regression model specific to each series individually, rather than applying a monolithic model to all dimensions simultaneously. To mitigate the risk of overfitting in scenarios with limited data or complex trends, we formulate a self-supervised learning task that enables the model to differentiate local patterns from global structures, thereby achieving robust generalization. Empirical validation on both simulated and real-world datasets confirms that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives.

A comprehensive suite of atmospheric dispersion models was analyzed using a data-driven approach. These models were on-sky measured via a dual-differential High-Resolution Atmospheric Dispersion Corrector (ADC) mounted at the VLT/UVOITS interface, specifically targeting the region between 550 nm and 750 nm. The validation of the various spectral-free atmospheric models involved the UVOITS package by comparing model predictions of the angular dispersion rate against these sky-based datasets. The study reveals that while all five evaluated models perform well for high dispersion angles (>0.3 arcseconds), they exhibit noticeable deviations from the measured data at lower dispersion angles (<0.2 arcseconds). Furthermore, a new, empirically derived ADC-based dispersion rate function offers superior accuracy over the pre-existing solar atmospheric models across the entire observation range.

Pre-trained language models have emerged as vital components of recent ranking systems, delivering superior performance at the expense of substantial computational requirements. Knowledge distillation offers a viable remedy for these challenges by transferring insights from an expert "teacher" network to a more compact "student" network, significantly enhancing the learner's efficiency without compromising accuracy. However, existing teachers often suffer from excessive architectural complexity, which hampers effective knowledge transfer to student models. In this paper, we introduce Progressively-weighted Input-Lexical aEnsemble for teacher dissolution (PILE), a novel multi-teacher distillation framework. PILE constructs iterative sequences of lightweight teachers designed to distill knowledge step-by-step. The framework employs a dynamic strategy that selects teacher inputs based on a attention mechanism for unlabeled data, while applying equal weighting to logs for labeled samples. Complementary to this, a balanced fusion mechanism ensures key features are maintained across a progressively deep network of teachers. Additionally, a smooth transition process facilitates seamless handover of learning signals between successive teacher stages. Empirical evaluations on the MS MARCO benchmark demonstrate that our method achieves significant improvements over the existing Baseline-R18 architecture.

Ultralight bosonic dark matter (UBDM) can be represented as a wave-like field characterized by a wavefunction with a globally conserved phase that undergoes slow drifts due to intrinsic dynamics and external influences. Similar to photons, UBDM fields generate detectable correlations between the flux variations of separate detectors, a signature known as quantum (or intensity) interferometry, a method applicable to various astrophysical sources. This interferometric correlation arises because, fundamentally, UBDM constitutes the collective excitation of a conserved charge, leading to emission events that are, to a large extent, correlated. Consequently, even though these events occur on astrophysical scales (such as galaxy or galactic cluster environments) and are rarely, they still produce an observable signal. By analyzing these subtle interferometric patterns, it becomes possible to derive constraints on UBDM properties based on the measured correlation strengths of UBDM-induced flux fluctuations from large-scale cosmic events.

This study investigates a one-dimensional inverse Radon transform in a continuous setting. We establish that the Basis Pursuit formulation possesses a unique solution when the underlying data features generic noise or a generic density. Furthermore, we analyze two integral-theoretic conditions on the data that are sufficient to guarantee Basis Pursuit uniqueness; we also provide a practical criterion relating noise and grid parameters under which a Basis Pursuit unique solution yields a piecewise constant approximation. Finally, we present numerical experiments supporting these theoretical findings.

The P4 language, a widely adopted solution for writing programmable switches, primarily functions as an independent, language-agnostic specification where specific compilation toolchains for various hardware platforms remain a limiting factor. This study introduces an open-source P4 compiler backend dedicated to reconfigurable match-per-group (MPG) table switches, which utilize a separate MPG stage to manage group actions within standard P4 match-based tables. This architectural approach streamlines the logic complexity often found in modern, high-performance switch specifications, which can otherwise become unwieldy. By leveraging the internal switch logic, a simple configuration process applies grouped execution policies, significantly reducing the programming overhead compared to manually mapping individual actions to multiple tables. To validate the feasibility of P4 specifications on MPG architectures, we developed a comprehensive toolchain compatible with V1-Main, 1.4, and 1.5 (of the V1 model), allowing the simulation of these designs on the industry-leading Broadcom TomoX2 platform. This research provides a robust foundation for both the evolution of the P4 language and the expansion of its supporting ecosystem.

In finite element simulations of incompressible fluid dynamics, a common discretisation scheme employs Raviart-Thomas elements of order zero for velocity and simple lowest-order elements for pressure on quadrilateral meshes. Despite the mixed finite element method demonstrating robust performance for many problems involving these 2D QRT0/LSL combinations, the accuracy significantly degrades when applied to the "vector transport equation," particularly due to a mismatch in polynomial degrees between the pressure and the convolved velocity pressure term (which elevates to order one). To address this, the study introduces two strategies: modifying element definitions to enforce a more accurate approximation of vector transport by equalizing polynomial degrees across velocity pressure terms, and utilizing a more sophisticated numerical integration rule for the discrete formulation. Both methods were comprehensively evaluated through various tests covering linear stability, with and without a stabilising penalty term, and linear and non-linear (Burgers-type) stability assessments, the latter examined both stabilised and unstabilised conditions.

The significant achievements driven by deep learning have introduced numerous ethical challenges, including algorithmic bias and threats to data privacy. To confront these issues, scholars employ techniques such as fairness evaluation metrics, federated learning architectures, and differential privacy. Initial research presented here introduces an ethical model integrating these three strategies simultaneously and uses experimentation across the Adult, Bank, and Dutch data sets to illuminate how a practical balance exists among accuracy, fairness, and privacy.

Analysis of $pp$ collision data, totaling an integrated luminosity of $10~\text{fb}^{-1}$ at $\sqrt{s}=13~\text{ TeV}$ by LHCb, reveals evidence for an excited $B_c^+$ state. Decaying via the $J/\psi\pi$ channel, this new state exhibits a mass of $6870.2 \pm 1.0 \pm 2.3 ~\text{GeV}/c^2$ with a significance of $9.0\sigma$. Its observed width is $48^{+9}_{-7}~\text{MeV}$. The subsequent analysis of spin and parity correlations, along with comparisons to predictions for the $2^{3}D_J$ and $3^{1}P_J$ muody modes of the $B_c$ meson, indicates that the $2^{3}S_1$ interpretation aligns best with the data. Recent advances in efficiently solving Hamiltonian numerics resulted in introducing a family energy-conserving Runge-Kutta techniques called Hamiltonians Runge-Kutta Boundary-Integral Methods. This new method class has interesting properties related to continuous-stage Runge-Kutta techniques that were revisited here for a broader range of general derivatives problems.

Model parallel deep neural networks (DNNs) are essential for training extremely large-scale architectures, as they enable models exceeding the memory limits of individual GPUs. A primary obstacle in this model-parallel training (MPT) pipeline is communication overhead, which can become a bottleneck for DNNs larger than a few hundred layers. Although distributed training often relies on a "critic" network to guide learning, the standard approach of copying layers from the main network into a single GPU incurs two drawbacks: first, it underutilizes available multi-GPU resources; second, it forces all layers to fit into limited high-bandwidth memory, causing the training of deep networks to depend on slow high-latency, low-bandwidth interconnects. In response, this paper introduces Local Critic Training (LCT), a strategy that distributes critic subnetworks across multiple GPUs to overcome the first limitation. The experimentals demonstrate that LCR significantly reduces the latency cost associated with the low-bandwidth components of MPT. Our MPT system utilizes heterogeneous GPUs with varying configurations, including different network widths and depths within the model, allowing it to train large-scale networks of unprecedented scale. Additionally, this paper outlines an analysis of how increasing the number of GPUs affects both training convergence and final model accuracy.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered significant attention across physics and chemistry disciplines, though much of the existing literature focuses exclusively on conservative (non-dissipative) systems. By investigating simple dissipative three-dimensional systems subject to low levels of dissipation, we demonstrate that weak dissipation can both generate and enlarge Wada fractals within the parameter space governing transient chaos. Our analysis reveals two distinct dissipation-driven mechanisms responsible for the formation of Wada boundaries: the disintegration of homoclinic globi and the decomposition of heteroclinic globi linking unstable periodic orbits situated on boundary basins. Additionally, we observe that increasing the degree of dissipation enlarges the scale at which these Wada fractals manifest.

We investigate a simple model where an accidental symmetry governs two light bosons, resulting in their longevity. Although these bosons alter quark flavors and generate observable electroweak instabilities, modifying them directly is prohibited, allowing us to explore indirect signatures via meson-meson mixing in the context of the first two generations of quarks. We analyze the implications of this framework on baryon oscillations and decay processes, as well as meson mixing within the $B_nB_s$D, and KS-K system. Furthermore, we examine charged boson-mediated tree-level interactions affecting the b, b, c, u, d, and s quarks, as this constitutes a testable region of parameter space. Our findings indicate that while such a model remains viable given current experimental limits, it remains difficult to confirm with present-generation detectors.

Recognizing human actions in unstructured video remains a difficult computer vision challenge. Existing methods typically address this by constructing two-level networks: a top segment network to extract action segments and a bottom CNN to analyze frames. However, current research limits attention mechanisms solely to the CNN component. This study introduces a Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN) equipped with a dual-attention architecture to identify and track spatiotemporal actions. The proposed system utilizes two parallel attention modules, a temporal attention unit that detects active regions within video segments, and a spatial attention unit sensitive to the duration of those regions. During the training phase, action segments are predicted at each scale to identify active movements, while the temporal unit pinpoints specific active regions, and the spatial unit highlights significant features, effectively minimizing unnecessary computational load. This hierarchical design enhances the model's interpretability and learning capability by integrating attention across both space and time. Comprehensive evaluations on the UCf100 and UCF-101 datasets confirm that the HAN achieves state-of-the-art performance.

This piece provides a brief overview of the principles surrounding star formation and its evolution based on observational evidence, showing that it is particularly meaningful in this light as the creation of planets is simply a side effect of stellar processes. Consequently, the entire inquiry regarding life throughout the universe and its origins can be approached from an innovative standpoint.

While Shannon entropy and associated metrics like mutual information are fundamental in data science, their estimation for moderate- to high-dimensional datasets poses significant challenges, particularly due to the difficulty in performing the necessary integration over high-dimensional spaces. This work proposes leveraging Nested Sampling to compute these entropies and mutual information directly from data points without requiring grid-based or sampling-based approximations that typically hinder accuracy in higher dimensions. We validate the introduced methodology through simulations across various distribution types and real-world datasets, demonstrating that for problems involving more than moderate dimensions, our approach outperforms existing sampling-grid and sampling-based estimators in terms of both precision and computational efficiency.

We analyze a specific nonlinear conservative hyperbolic equation featuring a quadratic flux. Given that the initial data is a finite vector-measure, we establish the existence of an entropically admissible solution in the context of distribution functions by employing a discrete $L^1$-approximation of the measure combined with a flux-limiter scheme. Additionally, assuming the measure has bounded variation and the initial data satisfies a condition of "compatibility," uniqueness of the solution can be demonstrated. This result is achieved by tightening the total variation bound through a novel "measure-mapping" technique and subsequently applying a standard Greenberger-type argument.

Cyber security is a pressing concern for organizations, given the escalating sophistication of modern attacks. While machine learning offers promising solutions, developing *effective* and *efficient* classifiers remains a significant challenge. Our proposed NB coded-DOs (NB coded-based Decision Making for Open Systems with Integrated Detection) approach equips resource-constrained IoT devices with the capability to identify specific Network Attacks using simple, low-overhead classifiers. The system leverages a Naïve Bayes classifier, which utilizes encoded representations of attack signatures within its conditional probability distributions—specifically based on a hashed bit-set encoding scheme. By encoding these signatures, the method ensures the maintenance of sufficient classifier accuracy even when employing this streamlined model on devices limited in computational power and storage. Our evaluation, which compared NB coded strategies against state-of-the-Large models on identical resources (in terms of speed and memory usage), demonstrated a significant performance improvement, establishing the efficiency of NB coded systems as fast as 80 percent relative to their complex counterparts.

Accurately identifying locomotion in surveillance footage is a difficult task, as current methods that depend on skin-tone segmentation, silhouette analysis, or re-identification fail when subjects are unrestrained, unshowered, or camouflaged. This study presents a solution by introducing BiLo—a binary classifier that distinguishes moving biological entities from inanimate objects. The model is built on the unique gait characteristics of biological locomotion, which operate at micro-meters per second scales and follow consistent 2-D periodic trajectories within an image's coordinate system. Empirical results indicate that this biological locomotion signature remains robust even under significant occlusion. BLo outperforms existing techniques on the challenging VisDrone20Lant dataset, where many inputs feature total silhouette loss. On that same dataset with clean bounding boxes—conditions where other methods typically excel—BLo still improves performance by 10%. Furthermore, when applied to the more complex Traffic dataset, which features small targets and cluttered backgrounds, BLo achieves state-of-the-art scores.

Optimizing power network resource allocation represents a vital component of smart grid operations to ensure efficient network functioning. We investigate this optimization challenge with a focus on quantum solution methodologies. By formulating the problem using Lagrangian duality to derive estimates for optimization objectives, we utilize the Bose-Liouville equation within the context of quantum density matrices to construct the duality gap evolution model. Leveraging the properties of quantum operators, we establish bounds for both the primal and dual objectives. Furthermore, we introduce an optimization algorithm capable of achieving a specified relative precision within quadratically fewer iterations compared to conventional approaches. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our proposed scheme through numerical simulations.

Machine learning offers significant potential for extracting knowledge from information, including the detection, separation, and characterization of various phenomena within images or mathematical functions. A central objective is discovering a universal model that generalizes effectively across domains; however, such discoveries are frequently complicated by anomalies that deviate from universality. These deviations may be intrinsic, intrinsic variations inherent to the system, or extrinsic causes such as measurement errors or environmental noise. While eliminating extrinsic factors is essential for accurate model identification, distinguishing intrinsic variations from extrinsic ones often poses a significant challenge. This review explores current methodologies for identifying universal laws and discrepancies, with a specific focus on approaches where the source of anomalies is unknown or ambiguous regarding their nature.

This analysis examines a data sample of proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV from the LHC's Run 2 period, collected by ATLAS and reaching a total integrated luminosity of 36.0 fb$^{-1}$. The study targets scenarios involving long-lived heavy charged particles that deposit significant energy. Such models arise in various extensions of the Standard Model, including those featuring heavy dark matter candidates or fractional charges. The specific search strategy examines the distinctive $\text{dE/dz}$ signature of these particles within ATLAS's Silicon Pixel Subsystem (SPC), combined with constraints on specific final-state particles. Results are interpreted through the lens of simplified dark sector models characterized by retuning interactions, as well as R-parity conserving supersymmetry. The analysis establishes 95% confidence level exclusion limits: simplified dark matter models with lifetimes of 1 ns are ruled out for masses up to 62.5 GeV, extending this reach to 625 GeV for 10 ns lifetimes. Similarly, simplified dark matter models exclude masses reaching 625 GeV for 1 ns lifetime and 6250 GeV for 100 ns at the same confidence level. The corresponding exclusions for R-parity conserving supersymmetry now cover stop quarks up to 425 GeV and stau squarks up to 425 GeV.

This study introduces theoretical and experimental evidence regarding ridge waveguide-based quantum dot single-photon emitters on chip platforms, achieving record-breaking, near-unity collection efficiency in the circuit frame of reference. We demonstrate an effective strategy to eliminate the efficiency bottleneck traditionally caused by coupling to planar interfaces by instead integrating a bottom mirror situated directly beneath the quantum dot. This approach supports in-plane interactions within the exciton-phonon system, facilitating the essential resonant strong coupling necessary for this emission method. Furthermore, we establish circuit-level near unity collection efficiency by matching the emitter's scattering spectrum with a tailored spectral response of the nanofabricated superconducting quantum interference device (SQID) readout. The theoretical and experimental consistency confirms that this architecture offers a universal pathway for significantly boosting the raw performance of in chip single-photon source technologies.

Inelastic neutron scattering offers a superior method for investigating low-energy excitations in glasses compared to other techniques. While the traditional view attributes these excitations to an anharmonic optical phonon mode occurring below the transverse sound wave cutoff frequency—a perspective that relies on the density of states showing a divergence at these low energies—our neutron scattering data for SiO₂ suggest a distinct interpretation. Specifically, we show that a part of these excitations is elastic, as evidenced by energies remaining constant across the examined q-range. This elasticity arises from atoms migrating within a cluster of roughly ten sites, as indicated by motion on a timescale of picoseconds. Although these excitations are quantum mechanical in nature, their existence does not necessitate anharmonic behavior. We propose that such phenomena may also account for the boson peak observed in the inelastic neutron scattering dynamic structure factor.

Contemporary experiments at particle physics facilities frequently involve observables that exhibit significant deviations from Standard Theory predictions; addressing these discrepancies demands the confrontation between theory and experiment with greater theoretical precision. Consequently, there is a growing necessity to broaden both the energy energy scales and the ranges of momentum transfers accessible in precision calculations. Realizing these goals involves advancing the complexity of such computations by integrating higher loop orders and a wider variety of particles, and simultaneously expanding the domains of valid valid scales and varying momentum regimes. Presently, physicists face significant challenges in managing intricate topologies of Feynman graphs, elevating calculation orders of perturbation expansions, and handling multi-scale characteristics within multi-loop frameworks effectively. To address these hurdles, this article examines key obstacles and corresponding responses regarding the evaluation of multi-loop multi-scale Feynman integrals, essential factors which underpin the evolution of precision in physics.

In systems involving energy deposition, certain combinations of wavefronts propagate outward at the eigenvalues of the scattering matrix, which correspond to the deposition rates in distinct spatial channels. During Scatttering events, these channels function as independent entities, resulting in total energy deposition equating to the sum of contributions from each individual channel. This study establishes various sum rules that relate the properties defined in the body to the spectrum of the energy deposition Hermitian operator acting on the scattering system's invariant subspace. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the sum of the phase shifts of all outgoing channels at resonance frequencies directly correlates to the real parts of the eigenvalues of this operator. Additionally, we derive novel connections for scatttering systems constrained to two dimensions, ensuring that every imaginary component of the resonance outgoing channel wavelengths directly reflects the sum of projection terms of their wavelength wavenummers.

We have identified the Far 3-kpc Arm, a novel spiral arm located within the Milky Way situated 2–3 kiloparsecs away from the galactic center. This discovery stems from the comprehensive mapping of the inner and mid-planes of the Galaxy by the Fundamental Plane Velocity Field Initiative (FPMI-FGS), which provides a detailed view of molecular gas motions across galactic scales. The new arm runs along a trajectory from the galactic center through the constellation Cassiopeia outwards. Kinematic data indicate that the Far Arm exhibits a distinct angular position relative to the kinematic bar structure, appearing to cross or connect with the kinematic arm branches near the galactic center. However, at a galactic circumferential distance exceeding 400 parsecs, the arm's angular position aligns closely with that of the Perseus Arm. Additionally, we have refined the angular position of the central bar to $28.5 \pm 0.5$ degrees based on these observations.

The growing interest in applications like drug design and image segmentation has driven a shift in Evolutionary Strategy (ES) research toward maintaining population diversity. While prior studies often qualitalively observe diversity improvements, this study investigates evolutionary mechanisms through a new quantitative metric: phenotypic diversity within a morphological framework. The entropy calculated from the probability distribution within local phenotypes—where a local phenotype comprises the paired outcomes of a parental genotype after non-parametric Gaussian perturbation—serves as the core of this proposed measure. The resulting metric effectively captures local diversity relative to parental genetic routes and reveals the mechanism by which ES fosters diversity. Specifically, it demonstrates that ES generates a more varied phenotype when selection pressure remains low and recombination is permitted. The findings confirm through ES experiments on the High-dimensional Elliptical Function and a synthetic Drone Routing task that enhancing diversity can significantly boost overall performance.

The concept of matching in stable rooms has recently expanded into three dimensions: given two matching contexts, such as job candidates for roles within a specific department at various universities, we seek a pair of matches for every instance. Addressing this challenge is difficult, even for simple additive preferences, as many potential match combinations must remain viable. However, if these preferences exhibit convexity, the problem decomposes into feasible ranges for each participant. This paper investigates 3D stable matchings under additive and convex assumptions to analyze the properties of preference sets that admit solutions and to establish an algorithm capable of finding one. Specifically, for cases where preferences are purely additive and independently generated from a uniform distribution on a known domain of possible partners at each university, we demonstrate that our method successfully produces a stable room assignment with near-certain reliability.

We introduce a comprehensive framework to investigate how electron-phonon (EP) interactions influence valley physics in two-dimensional systems. Notably, phonons can induce spin-polarized transport and a valley-polarized current, even when time-reversal symmetry holds for linearized electronic states. In this regime, the valley pseudomagnetic origin stems from the curvature of such states, the chirality of the coherent loop formed by electrons and phonons, and the deformation of electronic contours in momentum space caused by phonons. Moreover, the magnitude of the phonon-induced valley pseudomagnetic field is directly linked to the anisotropic deformation of these contours and to the non-adiabatic transformation between lattice deformation and electronic motion. To illustrate these principles, we applied the proposed formalism to graphene and MoS$_2$, calculating carrier distributions, pseudospectral densities, and valley pseudomagnetic fields. Consequently, we anticipate that phonon-mediated transport phenomena will drive the development of innovative transport devices based on van der Waals materials.

The paper proposes designing millimeter-wave (mm-wave) microstrip array elements capable of achieving extensive bandwidth and broad angular coverage. The analysis begins with the electromagnetic characteristics of an idealized infinite ground-plane-backed periodic array of circular patches situated in free space. Currently regarded as the sole practical pathway for large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing, the surface code relies on rapid and adaptable decoding algorithms capable of handling experimentally observed faulty syndrome measurements. This paper demonstrates that decoding under fully realistic fault-tolerant constraints can be elegantly reframed as an episodic reinforcement learning task. Consequently, neural networks trained via deep Q-learning emerge as highly effective decoding agents. We evaluate these learned decoders against standard established methods and find them to be at least as precise, while offering distinct advantages in terms of speed and adaptability to varying noise environments.

We introduce a method for quantum metrology that relies exclusively on monitoring the discrete jumps occurring within an ensemble of qubits interacting with the environment, with no information obtained from the drift component of the pure states. To demonstrate, we examine an optical microcavity system experiencing microcavity laser pumping and where the environment-induced jumps reflect the presence of quantum emission. This process enables precision measurement of a specific parameter governing the intracavity phase shift through an optimal strategy utilizing only this jump-based information. Notably, we discover that the ideal method achieves accuracy proportional to the square root of the number of participating qubits, achieving a precision level unattainable by traditional methods that rely solely on detecting the final state after many jump-free experiments.

The PHENIX collaboration reports findings on the jet-photon asymmetry within Au+Au and d+Au collisions during their run at RHIC operating at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. Analyses of d+Au collisions indicate a medium devoid of such interactions, though d-atomic effects are observed to influence high-$p_{\rm{T}}$ jets with a lower impact at lower transverse photon momenta. Furthermore, extending these photons-hadron correlations into Au+Au encounters reveals significant modifications in the jet-phadron $p_{\rm{T}}$ distributions across all investigated photon $p_{\rm{T}}$ ranges. The observed shifts in the jet $p_{\rm{T}}$ spectrum are largely consistent with expectations derived from parton energy loss mechanisms.

We investigate an analog-digitalhybrid framework in quantum computation that enables any quantum algorithm using alternative two-qubit approaches based solely on single-qubit rotations between dual bases on universal quantum processors. The proposed two-base approach demands fewer quantum gates than established Clifford and Pauli-based techniques, facilitating faster access to targeted states with higher fidelity or allowing shorter cycle implementations to yield better accuracy.

There has long existed a conflict in machine learning between models that generalize well and those that are highly efficient; that is, requiring only a limited number of parameters to achieve top performance. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have largely resolved this issue, but current models continue to exceed what might reasonably be considered parameter-efficient. This study introduces RFC, a technique for building additional features, aimed specifically at parameter efficiency. By simultaneously addressing the representation, optimization, and generalization aspects of the dilemma, this approach enables smaller neural networks to match the accuracy of larger ones. Crucially, the method requires no modifications to the existing architecture, making it broadly applicable to many popular systems. Empirical evaluations confirm that this construction strategy significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across numerous benchmarks.

These capabilities support advanced applications in photochemical therapy, photodynamic therapy, and advanced imaging.

Active experiments designed to measure neutrino oscillations can also probe sterile neutrinos within specific regions of the mass-mixing parameter space. Focusing on the DUNE project, this study evaluates its capacity to detect sterile states weighing less than 1 eV and masses extending up to several GeV. At heavier masses, signatures typically emerge in the near-detector responses; conversely, discoveries among lighter states demand signatures in the distant detector. Consequently, our analysis examines the relevant event topologies in both DUNE targets, estimating the sensitivity regarding neutrino-soliton mixing angles using simulated event samples. Ultimately, this research establishes the boundary lines between the near- and far-detector optimization zones in the sterile neutrino mass-mixing framework and quantifies DUNE's projected sensitivity across these distinct regimes.

Meta-analyses often involve studies that examine the same clinical trial in multiple ways, typically resulting in several effect size estimates. While it is standard practice to acknowledge this overlap by grouping such analyses together, ignoring the resulting dependence can lead to underestimated standard errors and the false inflation of statistical significance. Consequently, cluster-robust variance estimation (CRVE) has become an essential technique for addressing this issue in a broad spectrum of statistical models. Although CRVE is widely used in conventional statistics, its application in meta-analysis remains limited, particularly regarding the lack of closed-form solutions in existing closed-set estimators for dependent meta-meta-regression. This paper fills that gap by deriving a closed-form solution for CRVE within a two-level random-effects meta-regression framework and extending it to account for spatially autocorrelated residuals and small-sample adjustments. Furthermore, the authors evaluate these new methods against alternative variance techniques—such as those based on stack, cluster, or bivariate regression structures—through simulations and an application analyzing the mortality impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on over 100 studies covering more than 1.2 million individuals.

Particle-resolved simulation methods, such as resolved discrete element method and particle-resolved numerical method, are capable of capturing a wide range of multi-phase transport phenomena and are applicable to various engineering problems. A primary limitation for these methods remains the restriction on the simulation time-step imposed by contact stability. This paper introduces a novel algorithm that allows for the use of a time-step significantly larger than traditional limits by incorporating a physical criterion. The method features a two-phase structure: first, sub-cycles advance both the fluid-fluid interface and the fluid-solid interaction using small time-steps. Subsequently, a remapping step occurs to ensure mass, momentum, and other conserved quantities are properly accounted for. By utilizing contact forces to identify overlapping particles, the proposed method maintains accuracy in force transmission despite the enlarged global time-step. Validation tests were conducted on a single particle falling through a fluid environment. Results demonstrate excellent computational efficiency, with the ability to integrate time-steps up to 100 times greater than standard methods.

This study examines the energy origin of radiation in the Unruh and Hawking effects, with a focus on defining particle count based on conservation laws. The findings indicate that particle emission stems from disparities in how different observers define particle number due to conservation laws, rather than gravitational-force-induced pair creation. Specifically, radiated energy originates in the asymptotic limit, corresponding zero-point vibrations at effectively infinite wave numbers. Consequently, it becomes evident that models for black hole evaporation should be reconceptualized.

This study investigates the $x$-dependent evolution of the color dipole $N(N)$ function, where $N$ denotes the total number of partons. Within this framework, parton transverse momenta arise from the evolution operator. By assuming an exponential form for this operator, which aligns with the standard BFKL evolution of parton densities, we derive an expression for the distribution of transverse momentum imbalances ($q_T$) of dipole systems. This analysis reveals two key properties: (1) $q_T$ distributions exhibit a power-law behavior at small values with an exponent proportional to the BFKL eigenvalue, and (2) they show an exponential rise at large $q_T$ values governed by the saturation scale. By employing numerically evaluated $x$-dependent dipole distributions, we compute predictions for the distribution of transverse momentum imbalances in $pp$ collisions at the LHC. Our results suggest that significant $q_T$ asymmetries will be observable experimentally, providing evidence for enhanced transverse momentum broadening as gluons approach the saturation regime.

Ensuring fault tolerance and result correctness are paramount in High-Performance Computing (HPC). While RAM offers fast access, it remains vulnerable to failures; conversely, Next-Generation Non-Volatile Main Memory (NVMM) provides persistent storage for working sets but operates significantly slower. Aligned with industry trends toward broader NVMM adoption, we introduce the Algorithm-Directed Crash (ADC) model. Unlike traditional HPC approaches where algorithms assume volatile memory, the ADC paradigm utilizes main memory's non-volatile capability, allowing algorithms to explicitly manage crashes and recovery processes. Initially, as an HPC runtime environment integrating the MPI standard, our implementation has been tested on HPC benchmarks ranging from machine-wide to task-level scales. Empirical evaluations confirm that the realizable fault tolerance overhead remains minimal and that the ADC model successfully guarantees both algorithm- and MPI-correctness following random mid-execution faults caused by power loss.

This study introduces a class of hierarchical models designed to capture both the structure and characteristics of expansive, hierarchically organized networks. We extend the Multilayered Preferential Attachment model, originally proposed by Kim and Eoh, by incorporating a hierarchical framework into its attachment mechanisms. By employing a technique akin to hierarchical Dirichlet processes, we allocate attachment rules across various scales; this process can subsequently be estimated using standard Gaussian Mixture Models via the EM algorithm. Empirical analysis of real-world datasets confirms the models' capacity to represent multi-level hierarchies inherent in complex information structures. Furthermore, we prove convergence in distribution for these hierarchical networks as the system grows, demonstrating that their local structures asymptotically match a specific stochastic graph known as the Multi-Preferential Graph.

We introduce a method for generating probability density functions (PDFs) applicable to three-particle systems. These PDFs are derived from invariant characteristics of the configuration space—specifically, null-conformal equivalents of the configuration manifold and its metric expressed in terms of special coordinates known as Fux variables. By applying a generalized statistical model originally proposed by B. Schoemans for one-dimensional $N$-particle systems, we derive corresponding PDFs for any set of variables respecting the conservation of energy, momentum, and angular momentum in $D$ spatial dimensions. These dimensionally adjusted distributions were then tested against the outcomes of three-body simulations. We found significant discrepancies when the predicted PDFs were compared to the actual results of these simulations.

Measurements of nuclear modification factors ($R_{AA}$) for $J/\psi$ mesons in lead-lead collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 5.02$ TeV are examined in this study. Comparisons are made against mid-central and centrality $p$-pb collisions, as well as no-collisions references. The measurement spans 13 rapidity bins ranging from $y= -6.0$ to $+ 6.0$, with results presented in two ways: bin-by-bin for $|y| < 3.5$ and bin-by-bin for $ 3.5$. Distinguishing measurements for prompt $J/\psi$ (derived from decays not associated with long-lived beauty hadrons) and nonprompt $J/\psi$ (primarily stemming from $B$-meson decays) offer insights into quarkonium suppression mechanisms within the quark-gluon plasma. Uncertainties associated with the quark-gluon plasma QCD calculations are substantial; however, this work provides the first comprehensive, bin-by-bin determination of $R_{AA}$ for $ 3.5$, which offers a more thorough constraint on quark-gluon plasma models.

We propose defining predicate orderings within certain categories to construct a new form of logical topology. This approach establishes a topology-of-continuity, ensuring that all logical structures vary continuously with respect to an embedded spatial topology. Our development extends the methodologies pioneered by Macintyre, Rosendal, and Moyal to a broader range of cases. Within this framework, the subobjects of a formula function as "truth values," representing the extent to which a statement holds at any continuous level; these truth values subsequently induce a spatial topology. Moreover, the interpretants of all logical expressions emerge as morphisms equipped with a specific topological structure. Notably, the resulting topology may vary even when the underlying category remains unchanged, though in instances involving metric spaces, this topology generalizes the classical Gaudin topology—often referred to as the Gaudin topology in literature, though here we refer to it regarding lower semi-continuous properties.

In software system development, modifying a specific component can inadvertently trigger detrimental changes elsewhere, potentially harming system performance. Regression testing is employed to verify unaffected modules and mitigate this risk, yet the vast number of test cases in such systems makes manual selection difficult. To address this, the Test Case Selection (TCS) algorithm was developed to utilize Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) for selecting cases that best cover system features, thereby maximizing regression efficiency. This study introduces a parallelized SVD-based TCS algorithm, and its performance was evaluated against sequential approaches. Experimental results demonstrated that the parallel version of the SVD-TCS approach is faster than traditional sequential test selection methods, significantly reducing the time required to execute regression checks following system changes compared to existing solutions.

Recent research has revealed that icosahedral viruses, such as the bacteriophage $\lambda$, possess striking mechanical resilience when subjected to extreme tensile stress, maintaining integrity up to a stretch of 20-fold their original size. We demonstrate in this study that the magnitude of that stretching is constrained by the virion's geometry, such that the virion's center-of-mass follows a closed loop via self-rolling, governed by its surface features. This self-rolling mechanism generates the virion's elastic energy, which in turn dictates the potential energy stored, while the available configuration space determines the system's entropy. We show this athermal, geometry-driven system can only remain stable when the virion is stretched beyond a specific geometric threshold, resulting in a sharp, switch-like stretching behavior. This self-rolling model, however, fails when the virion has a low surface area-to-volume ratio, which is the case for many large, modern viruses, thereby predicting the existence of different stretching regimes based on icosahedral symmetry and size. We conclude by exploring the biological potential of this self-rolling physics, particularly regarding force generation for intracellular transport and infection mechanisms through bacterial cell walls.

Three-dimensional topological insulators (TIs) are defined by a quantized magnetoelectric coefficient, yet this linear coupling cannot be directly realized in systems possessing time-reversal symmetry (TRS). In contrast, the nonlinear generalization of the magnetoelectric effect remains susceptible to detection in such symmetric states. This paper proposes an explicit theoretical model that yields a nonvanishing, quantized magnetoelectric coefficient within the quantum Hall regime at half-integer filling. We examine the Witten effect—charge quantization in Witten terms—within this framework and explore the implications of our findings for future experimental investigations.

While developers widely use discussions on platforms like GitHub for project planning, issue resolution, and feature exploration, the challenges associated with converting these unstructured texts into stable visual representations for issue tracking systems remain, as small variations in the underlying mining approach can produce significantly different graphs. To address this stability concern, we present a comprehensive evaluation framework that enables assumption-driven assessment, analysis, and conclusion stability assessment regarding graph representations derived from design dialogues. First, we validate the stability of using various text representations under the assumption that individual words correspond to distinct concepts; our results suggest that word embeddings fail to reliably replicate this stability compared to other popular encoding strategies such as TF-IDF or character n-grams. Next, we investigate the reproducibility of link structures in concept conversations under the assumption that words map to specific topics; this analysis reveals that standard keyword-mapping strategies also generate unstable links relative to topic-based alternatives. Finally, under the assumption that design dialogues follow coherent argumentative structures, our study concludes that keyword-outlined arguments exhibit greater stability when links are defined by the frequency of word co-mentions, surpassing the stability found in other methods for determining connection rules. Overall, our study assists researchers and developers in navigating the complex stability landscape of mining design discussions to achieve more stable graph outcomes.

Proximity algorithms are effective at identifying optimal solutions for convex optimization problems that involve constraints or nonsmooth elements by utilizing the proximal operator, while Newton methods efficiently determine optimal solutions for problems that are twice continuously differentiable. This research investigates conditions under which these two approaches can be integrated, specifically demonstrating that Proximal-Newton schemes are viable whenever the proximity mappings are restricted to specific subspaces of the argument space characterized by closed ranges and operator derivatives that are continuously dependent on the point, with this result applying broadly to a large category of subdifferential based Proximal-gradient schemes. Additionally, under specific constraints, we establish that Proximal-Newton schemes yield an effective method for solving equal constraint optimization problems where the Jacobian of the constraint functions has a closed range in the case of full rank.

This study defines weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals in commutative rings with identity and examines key properties. Finally, the paper presents specific examples to illustrate that the corresponding poset of subsets of $1$-absorbing prime ideals may fail to form a lattice, and it provides examples of nice rings in which these two concepts coincide.

The development of the high-velocity radial velocity technique, known as HCRT, relies on nonlinear spectral analysis within a mathematical framework. In this approach, computer-generated theoretical spectra serve as a basis for extracting velocity data from observed stellar spectra. The article introduces a design process for creating a new optical system tailored to HCRT, utilizing a grating-based spectrograph. To achieve this, the system operates on the principle of spectrograph, where light enters through an entrance aperture and exits through an exit aperture. The optical components are selected and optimized to produce a final spectrally compressed image at the detector plane, effectively reducing the wavelength range spread. Lately, various machine learning models designed to predict how potential drug combinations function have gained significant traction. These hybrid systems effectively merge the strengths of graph-based knowledge representation with inductive learning capabilities from tabular data sources. While prior studies have applied these principles to tasks like forecasting medication responses or identifying polypharmacological targets, this work offers a consolidated examination of relational deep learning methodologies for evaluating scores between current and candidate drug pairs. We investigate the architectural components driving these models, outline the key differences among existing systems, and assess their relative performance across four distinct benchmark datasets. Ultimately, this analysis aims to offer valuable direction for the development of novel drug discovery tools grounded in relational deep learning.

Identifying road damage and implementing repairs are critical municipal responsibilities, as infrastructure neglect can severely hamper transport efficiency and escalate economic costs. Historically, mapping road defects relied on expensive and laborious fieldwork. In contrast, this paper introduces a machine-learning framework that leverages telecentric camera images to detect road issues, employing the model to classify six common classes of damage. The proposed system utilizes a ResNet-101 convolutional neural network trained on the newly compiled, multi-national dataset, DODOS; this resource aggregates images from four distinct nations to enhance diversity and represent variability in road environments. By applying transfer learning with a pre-trained ResNet-101 model, the study achieves superior performance—surpassing previous state-of-the-art results of 1.7% to 2.1% in top-5 accuracy—while maintaining compact model sizes that facilitate efficient deployment on edge computing devices.

Imitation learning addresses the challenge of constructing effective reward functions for policy agents by leveraging expert demonstrations. While recent years have seen a surge of research, most approaches rely on high-level robotics data that are difficult to access in practical scenarios. Observational instead, this work takes on the challenge of learning policies through low-level, raw observations alone, drawing insights from the varying intrinsic rewards derived from different execution paths. By reformulating the problem as a maximization task for the expected minimum of these internal signals, we allow the agent to replicate behaviors without explicit expert instructions on "correctness." To solve this, we propose an improved Adversarial Observational Cross-Domain (iAODC) architecture that splits the problem into a discriminator, which identifies the distribution of optimal intrinsic rewards within observed trajectories, and a generator, which refines its policy to generate examples that deceive the discriminator by appearing as high-reward trajectories. Ultimately, we demonstrate that policies learned via iAODC from first-person observations significantly rival the performance of standard methods trained on the same expert data.

A critical unresolved issue regarding the early universe involves the birth of the first massive stars (Population III). Current theories suggest that at low metallicity, dust grains fail to provide sufficient radiative cooling, causing gas clouds to contract primarily until dust begins to form within a protostar. We investigate massive protostars reaching densities high enough for molecular hydrogen ($\text{H}_2$) to induce cooling. Our findings indicate that once the surrounding magnetic field is amplified exponentially by this dust-deprived environment, it reaches a state where magnetically supported scales are smaller than the Jeans length. Consequently, the gas cannot fragment into subsequent star-forming clumps, effectively halting further star birth. This process aligns with established mechanisms where magnetic fields are amplified in similar early-stage environments. Furthermore, if this mechanism operates, it suggests a pathway for Population III protostars to evolve into super-critical objects possessing extreme masses and masses exceeding the Eddington limit without collapsing. These findings underscore the necessity of incorporating magnetic fields into simulations of early massive star formation.

Individuals involved in criminal justice tend to exhibit poorer health compared to the general population, with limited understanding of the root causes. Multiple jurisdictions have implemented laws requiring convicted individuals to participate in mental therapy, though these programs suffer from high wait times that delay service delivery. By utilizing variation in these pre-existing mandated conditions—specifically the gaps between condition and fulfillment—as a "natural experiment," this research seeks "fuzzy" causal effects. The findings indicate mental health conditions among criminals are indeed partially linked to post-conviction access issues, with ultimate compliance occurring within a year. This study reveals that mental health problems among criminals are indeed worse than those seen in the general population prior to the enforcement period, suggesting that addressing these unmet needs significantly improves outcomes beyond what is observed when looking at just the enforcement period itself by considering a broader time frame.

This research introduces parameterized variations of generalized Apostol–Bernoulli polynomials alongside their corresponding generating functions, examines various properties and relationships within these polynomials, and establishes connections with additional special polynomial families.

Radio maps are increasingly recognized as a viable method for providing situational awareness in next-generation wireless networks. Their substantial value intensifies in dense urban environments where a lack of global positioning infrastructure exists. By utilizing these networks themselves as a source of spatial data for network and localization management, radio maps become indispensable for network optimization. To ensure robust location tracking and network services, we propose deploying autonomous unmanned aerial vehicles (UUVs) as mobile platforms for radio map estimation, noting that existing methods relying on ground or fixed towers are insufficient. Furthermore, since data collection occurs incrementally as the UAV flies, we address the challenge of real-time map updating. Consequently, we introduce a novel sequential map learning framework that integrates efficient communication and control strategies with an online Bayesian inference approach. This innovation allows for the construction of a unified map learning system that converges to the optimal solution while simultaneously enabling the control module to achieve consistent, collision-free flight with smooth trajectories. Extensive simulation results validate the proposed method's performance across various network configurations, demonstrating rapid Bayesian inference convergence, effective collision avoidance, and reasonable computational complexity relative to standard Bayesian inference techniques.

This study introduces a novel methodology for identifying faults in critical, fault-tolerant systems using Hidden Markov Models (HMMs). System performance is assessed via multi-sensor data, where each measurement is processed through an HMM to estimate the system's likely hidden state; discrepancies between these states signify anomalies. The developed approach handles multi-sensor inputs by constructing a composite model capable of handling data-specific transformations. Experimental validation utilizing historical fault injection tests from the Fault Injection Facility (FJI) at the European Space Agency (ESA)—involving a fault diagnosis system built from a fan assembly—demonstrates that this method effectively detects systematic faults.

This study introduces a novel multimodal person verification system utilizing synchronized thermal imagery and video. We constructed the world's largest dataset featuring simultaneously captured thermal, audio-visual, and person metrics. This comprehensive collection, comprising over 1,000 individuals, was gathered using four distinct cameras: two providing high-resolution color imagery with integrated audio capabilities and two offering mid-resolution thermal scanning. We present the dataset's specifics, including a web-based search interface designed to facilitate the acquisition of biometric samples for every individual. Our research outlines a systematic methodology for performing person verification through this new multimodal dataset, achieving a successful success rate of 98.15% on the Labeled Face Swapped 39 (LFSV39) subset and a 61.19% success rate on the Extended CMT-39 subset of the Custom Multi-modal Person Dataset 1 (CMDP1). We also evaluate the effectiveness of various existing verification methods, establishing a robust baseline for future research into new verification systems that leverage thermal and audiovisual inputs.

Data augmentation has emerged as a vital technique for enhancing the performance and robustness of deep neural networks. Despite the well-documented advantages of augmentation, the performance gains for automatic speech systems are modest, and the computational and operational costs of creating diverse data types often discourage researchers from adopting it more widely. To address this, we present a method that requires minimal effort and requires no model retraining to derive significant performance improvements. Our approach involves simply adding noise to the input audio features and the associated text translations. By modeling noise as a convolutional kernel applied via element-wise operations, we demonstrate that this technique is fully compatible with attention-based neural architectures. Extensive experiments on large-scale speech and translation tasks reveal that our augmentation strategy is highly effective. Crucially, our method achieves an improvement of approximately 10% on the possible performance boost, significantly surpassing the typical 0.5% to 1.0% gains observed in typical data augmentation for speech recognition. This simple technique shows potential for immediate deployment in production environments.

We introduce a broad maximum likelihood approach for estimating the mixture component means. Under the assumption of known component variances and a bounded number of mixture components of fixed dimension, we demonstrate that the proposed estimator converges in distribution to the true parameter at the $\sqrt{n}$ rate. The standard asymptotic distribution consists of a weighted sum of multivariate normal distributions, where the weights correspond to the stationary class probabilities. Given that the estimator achieves this $\sqrt{n}$ consistency, the normal convergence structure allows for the development of a valid $n=n$ asymptotic confidence interval for each mean. These confidence intervals remain accurate even in the face of heavy-tailed data or an unlimited number of mixture types. The methodology for constructing these intervals is straightforward and involves maximizing a generalized likelihood function. The paper illustrates this technique using two scenarios: locating an optimal sampling site for freshwater quality assessment in the Great Lakes, and refining the sampling geometry for imaging the Moon's dark side using laser altimetry.

Ensuring privacy when releasing data about correlated or dependent features is a critical challenge. To address this, we extend the concept of one-sided differential privacy to depict the practical private release of datasets characterized by such dependencies. We provide sufficient conditions for one-sided differential privacy to hold regardless of the underlying data dependency, making it a feasible framework for releasing training data for common dependent models in real-world applications. Furthermore, we establish outer bounds for the set of all possible one-sided private mechanisms, similar to the capacity limits defined by differential privacy over non-dependent data. Finally, we evaluate the performance of rate matrices associated with discrete rate matrices for specific datasets exhibiting two typical dependencies: parity and Markov chains.
